newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: POWs die of disease in rebel-held Afghan prison.
newsitem.headline: POWs die of disease in rebel-held Afghan prison.

text.p: Prisoners of war held by Afghan rebels besieging the capital Kabul said on Wednesday there had been deaths from disease at the largest of a number of locations where the inmates are kept.

But the prisoners said doctors were allowed in to treat the inmates who died and officials of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) were regularly allowed to visit at least this camp, called Baraharak.
The camp was inspected by a small group of foreign journalists, including Reuters, on Wednesday.

Baraharak prison commander Alim Jan confirmed without hesitation the prisoners' accounts of five deaths from severe diarrhoea and tuberculosis over the past two months when tempratures soared to 45 degrees Celsius (113 F).

Jan said the forces of top northern alliance commander Ahmad Shah Masood were holding a total of 1,600 POWs at 10 locations in the Panjsher Valley, a rebel stronghold even during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
He said about 100 other prisoners, whom he described as "Pakistanis", were also held in a special high security prison in the valley.
Masood's northern alliance ally General Abdul Malik is believed to be holding about 5,000 POWs, including some "Pakistanis", in northern parts of Afghanistan.
Afghan opposition factions accuse neighbouring Pakistan of helping the government of the Islamic fundamentalist Taleban movement with arms and men. But Islamabad denies the charge.
The Taleban government also holds similar numbers of rebel prisoners, and POWs have become key bargaining chips in any possible negotiations to head off a final battle for Kabul.

During the visit to the camp, where 350 POWs are held in a mud compound 60 metres long by 30 metres wide, foreign journalists saw prisoners carrying out road works near the camp and going to a nearby river to bring back water.
The prisoners showed signs of recent medical treatment, including fresh-looking bandages on small cuts on toes and finers. They did not appear to be badly malnourished.
The prisoners are guarded by 40 rebel soldiers who lock them in dormitory rooms in the compound from 10 p.m. until 3.30 a.m., when they are allowed out of the dormitories.
The dormitories have windows and the prisoners sleep Afghan-style on mats on the earthen floor.
Two ICRC representatives, based near the prison, refused to answer any of reporters' questions about treatment of prisoners.

Jan said he was a lawyer in Kabul until he joined Masood's forces nine years ago. He said he also was a prisoner for four years in Kabul during the Soviet occupation and understood the pain and sufferings his present charges went through.
He said the prisoners were given three meals a day of bread, rice, beans and one or two times a week meat.
However, he again candidly admitted that because of food shortages throughout the valley due to war, there were weeks when the prisoners did not receive any meat at all.
"We are doing the best we can but, because supply routes are badly blocked, sometimes there is no meat for the prisoner or even for us," he said.
Ibrahim, who has been a prisoner at the camp for 2-1/2 months, said the main thing POWs needed was medical supplies to head off diseases like diarrhoea and tuberculosis.
He said some POWs were also worried about their fate when the bitterly cold Afghan winter grips the valley towards the end of the year.
